title: Pine Brook Hill Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Pine Brook Hill wells have a 125-foot median depth, with fractured mountain bedrock affecting yield and drilling cost.
h1: Pine Brook Hill Well Depth, Yield, and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Buying land in Pine Brook Hill means looking closely at the well, not just the house or access road. Records within five miles show a 125-foot median well depth, but the middle half ranges from 25 to 325 feet. That wide spread reflects mountain bedrock and changing site conditions.

Reported well yields are generally workable, with a 7.0 gallons-per-minute median. Most permitted wells are domestic or household wells, and most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. These records are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a new well will produce on a particular lot.

sections.heading: Pine Brook Hill Well Depths Reflect Fractured Mountain Ground
sections.html:
The local depth numbers cover a broad range. The median is 125 feet, while the middle half of reported wells falls between 25 and 325 feet. A well at the 90th percentile reaches 525 feet, and the deepest record is 4,550 feet. Nearly half of the wells are under 100 feet, while 22% are between 100 and 300 feet, 23% between 300 and 600 feet, and 8% exceed 600 feet.

For a driller's bid, the median is only a starting point. Pine Brook Hill is mountain terrain dominated by fractured granite and gneiss. A nearby shallow success does not prove that the same fracture system continues beneath your lot. Budgeting should allow for a site-specific depth decision, proper casing and grout, and the possibility that drilling goes substantially deeper than the local median.

sections.heading: What Pine Brook Hill Wells Usually Produce
sections.html:
Among wells with reported pump yields, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. The yield mix is encouraging for many household uses: 69% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 11% report more than 15 gallons per minute, 18% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 2% report under 1 gallon per minute.

That low-yield share is small, but it matters when evaluating a home or building lot. A yield test is more useful than a neighbor's verbal estimate. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, storage capacity, and any history of seasonal shortage. A well producing steadily at a modest rate can work with storage and careful household demand, while a high-flow result is not a substitute for water-quality testing.

sections.heading: Water Levels Are Variable, Not a Simple Dropping Trend
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a 26-foot median, with the middle half from 9 to 95 feet below ground surface. The decade medians vary sharply: 31 feet in the 1960s, 41 feet in the 1970s, 60 feet in the 1980s, 6 feet in the 2000s, 73 feet in the 2010s, and 12 feet in the 2020s.

This series does not show a dependable one-direction decline. The measurements move both shallower and deeper across decades, and only 152 wells report a static water level. Treat the numbers as local reference points rather than a complete groundwater trend. For a purchase, compare the subject well's measured water level with its pump setting, recent production history, and nearby wells at similar elevation.

sections.heading: Permit History and Drillers Around Pine Brook Hill
sections.html:
The records include 5,858 permitted wells, with 3,648 recorded as constructed. Permits span several generations: the largest decade was the 1990s with 1,008 permits, followed by 909 in the 1970s and 630 in the 1980s. There were 303 permits in the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 801 wells, Ground Water Systems Inc (Wilson, Richard R.) with 761, and Norris & Sons (Norris, T A) with 231. These counts describe permit records, not a recommendation or a guarantee of current availability. The use mix is mainly domestic or household at 63%, with monitoring wells at 23%, stock at 2%, and irrigation at 1%.

sections.heading: Pine Brook Hill Drilling Cost: What to Carry in the Budget
sections.html:
In fractured mountain bedrock such as granite and gneiss, the drilling rate is typically $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 125 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $8,100 to $12,500. That is not the complete water-system price.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,100 to $24,500 at the median depth. The final bid can change with access, casing and grout requirements, terrain, power distance, water testing, and actual depth. Ask the contractor to separate drilling from the pump system and site work. That makes it easier to compare bids and see which costs increase if the hole must go deeper.

sections.heading: Risks to Check Before Buying or Building
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are the main physical uncertainties in fractured bedrock. The records show 2% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, but the database covers only 896 wells with a reported pump yield. Missing information is not proof of either success or failure. Require the actual well report and a current flow or recovery test when possible.

Water quality also deserves a site-specific review. Within about ten miles are 103 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 652 historic mine features, and 67 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped locations do not establish contamination in a particular well, but they support testing for relevant contaminants. Before construction, verify septic setbacks, available drainfield area, well access for a rig, and the county and Colorado DWR requirements for the intended use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Pine Brook Hill?
faq.a: The median reported depth within five miles of Pine Brook Hill is 125 feet. The middle half ranges from 25 to 325 feet, while the 90th percentile is 525 feet. Nearly half are under 100 feet, but fractured granite and gneiss can produce much deeper wells, so nearby depth records should guide planning rather than set a guaranteed drilling depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Pine Brook Hill?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 125-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $8,100 to $12,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $14,100 to $24,500. Access, casing, grout, power distance, and final depth can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Pine Brook Hill?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 7.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 5.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. About 69% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. A small share, 2%, reports under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for a pump test and recovery history because only 896 wells report a yield.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Pine Brook Hill?
faq.a: The permit records do not prove that any individual well is safe to drink. Within about ten miles are 103 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 652 historic mine features, and 67 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well water for contaminants relevant to the property and its surroundings, and repeat testing when conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Does Pine Brook Hill have a declining water table?
faq.a: The available decade data does not show a simple, continuous decline. Median static water depth was 31 feet in the 1960s, 60 feet in the 1980s, 6 feet in the 2000s, 73 feet in the 2010s, and 12 feet in the 2020s. Only 152 wells report static levels, so use the subject well's recent measurements for a better comparison.
